opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a lovely case study, partly because mathematics was one of the first intellectual domains people tried to automate, and the story has been quite different from what people expected.

If you go back far enough, "computer" was a job title. There were rooms full of people, often women, doing long calculations by hand for astronomical tables, artillery tables, actuarial work and so on. That job was almost entirely automated away by mechanical and then electronic computers. But mathematicians themselves didn't disappear. What happened is that the routine part, the arithmetic, got peeled off, and the people doing the more conceptual work found they could do vastly more of it. Then the same thing happened again with computer algebra systems: symbolic integration and manipulating huge expressions, which used to be a real skill people were proud of, became something you'd just hand to Mathematica.

So the first lesson is that automation tends to come for tasks, not jobs. A job is a bundle of tasks, and the machine takes the most well-specified, checkable ones first. What's left often becomes more valuable, at least for a while.

The second lesson is about what we thought was hard. For a long time people assumed that calculation was the hard, intelligent bit and that things like judgment, taste, and deciding which problem is interesting were somehow softer. In fact, the hierarchy of difficulty for machines is quite different from the hierarchy of prestige for humans. That should make us humble about predicting which jobs are "safe."

But the third lesson, and I think the one that matters most now, is that this pattern of "the machine takes the bottom rung and humans move up" isn't a law of nature. It has held because each wave of automation was narrow. With modern AI systems, we're seeing them start to do things like competition mathematics and help with proofs, the very layer that mathematicians retreated to. If systems keep improving, there may be no next rung to climb to. The comforting historical story depends on there always being some residual task that humans do better, and with sufficiently general systems that assumption could just fail.

So I'd say mathematics teaches us both the reassuring story, that automation has historically augmented rather than replaced skilled thinkers, and also why we shouldn't extrapolate that story too confidently. The reassurance came from the narrowness of past tools, and narrowness is exactly what's changing.

r001.rationale: It says automation peeled off routine arithmetic, allowing mathematicians to do vastly more conceptual work.

r002.rationale: It mentions AI doing competition mathematics and helping with proofs, but does not suggest that automating proofs would free mathematicians to formulate new questions or theories.

r003.rationale: It describes jobs as bundles of tasks and explains that machines automate specified, checkable tasks first, leaving conceptual work that can be overlooked when focusing on the automated part.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really interesting case, because mathematics is in some ways the field where automation has the longest history. If you go back to the word "computer," that was originally a job description — a human computer was a person, often a woman, who sat in a room doing arithmetic by hand, calculating tables of logarithms or artillery trajectories or the positions of the planets. And that job was almost entirely automated away by mechanical and then electronic computers. So that's one data point: a whole category of intellectual labour just disappeared.

But what's striking is that it didn't make mathematicians obsolete. If anything, there are far more mathematicians now than there were then, and they're doing more interesting things. The arithmetic was the drudgery, and once you take the drudgery away, the people shift to the parts that are harder to automate — choosing which problems matter, finding the right framing, having the insight that connects two areas that nobody had connected before.

And then we've had further waves. Computer algebra systems like Mathematica took over a lot of symbolic manipulation — things that would have been considered real mathematical skill, integrating a nasty expression by hand. Computer-assisted proofs, like the four colour theorem, where the machine does a case analysis no human could check. And now with proof assistants like Lean, and increasingly with language models, you're getting systems that can actually do pieces of proof search, and in some cases solve competition problems at a very high level.

So I think there are a few lessons. One is that automation tends to come for the well-specified, mechanical parts first, and each time it does, people redraw the line of what counts as "real" mathematics. What was skilled work becomes something you'd be embarrassed to do by hand. That pattern probably generalises — in law, in medicine, in programming, the routine parts go first and the definition of the profession moves.

A second lesson, though, is that this comforting story might not hold forever. Each previous wave left a residue of things humans were clearly better at. The question with the current systems is whether that residue is shrinking in a qualitatively different way — whether you're now automating the insight, not just the execution. And I don't think we can read off from the history of mathematics that there will always be a human-shaped hole left over. The past hundred years of mathematical automation looks like a story of complementarity, but it could turn out to be the first part of a story of substitution, and you wouldn't be able to tell the difference until quite late.

And a third thing — which I think is underappreciated — is that mathematics is in some ways the easiest case for automation, because the ground truth is so clear. A proof is correct or it isn't, and a machine can verify that. Most jobs don't have that property. So if we see full automation in mathematics, that's not necessarily evidence that other jobs follow quickly — but it's also a sign of what's coming, because the verification problem is exactly the kind of thing people are working hard to solve elsewhere.

r001.rationale: The response says automation removed arithmetic drudgery and let mathematicians shift toward harder work.

r002.rationale: It discusses automated proof work and mathematicians choosing problems, but does not clearly connect proof automation to freeing them to formulate new questions or theories.

r003.rationale: It contrasts the automated arithmetic with mathematicians’ higher-level work, such as choosing important problems and finding new framings.

astra-6.text:
I think mathematics is a particularly interesting case because we’ve been automating parts of it for a very long time. And yet we still have mathematicians. That doesn’t show that we’ll always have mathematicians, but it does tell us something about how automation can change a job rather than simply eliminate it.

Think about arithmetic. Being able to perform calculations quickly and accurately used to be a much more valuable skill than it is today. We’ve largely handed that over to machines. But we don’t usually describe this as having automated mathematics. We think of mathematics as the interesting work that remains: deciding what questions to ask, finding the right concepts, understanding why something is true.

There’s a similar story even with notation. A good system of notation can turn something that required ingenuity into a procedure you can carry out almost mechanically. So mathematicians have, in a sense, been working to automate their own thinking for centuries. Once you understand something well enough, you try to make it routine, and then you use it to tackle something harder.

I think that’s a useful way to think about other jobs. A job is generally a collection of tasks, and automating some of those tasks can make the person doing the remaining ones much more productive. It can also open up work that previously wouldn’t have been worth attempting.

But there’s an important limit to that historical analogy. It doesn’t establish that there must always be another task for the human to move on to. If machines become better at choosing the questions and understanding the answers as well, then the situation could be quite different. So I’d take the history as a reason to be careful about equating the automation of a task with the disappearance of a profession, rather than as a guarantee that professions are safe.

r001.rationale: It says machines have taken over routine calculation and describes mathematicians’ remaining work as asking questions, finding concepts, and understanding proofs.

r002.rationale: It discusses automating calculations and notation, but does not suggest that automating mathematical proofs frees mathematicians to formulate new questions or theories.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes automating calculations from automating mathematics as a whole, pointing to the higher-level work that remains.

sol-6.1.text:
I think mathematics is a really interesting example because we’ve been automating parts of it for a very long time. The word “computer” used to refer to a person whose job was to perform calculations. Those jobs have largely disappeared, but mathematicians haven’t disappeared along with them.

What happened was that an activity which looked like a central part of mathematics turned out to be something we could hand over to machines. That allowed people to concentrate on other things: deciding which questions to ask, finding useful ways to represent a problem, and understanding what the answers mean.

And I think there are two lessons here which pull in different directions. One is that automating a task doesn’t necessarily mean automating the whole occupation. A job is a collection of different activities, and removing one of them can make the remaining activities more valuable. It can also make things possible that simply weren’t practical before.

But the other lesson is that this isn’t a guarantee that humans will always have something left to do. You can look at that history and say, “Well, we’ll just keep moving up to a higher level of abstraction.” But that depends on machines continuing to be unable to operate at that higher level. There’s no general principle that says they must stop there.

So I’d be wary both of saying, “This task can be automated, therefore the profession is finished,” and of saying, “Previous automation created new roles, therefore this will always happen.” The important question is which parts of the work remain a bottleneck, and whether humans retain an advantage at those parts.

r001.rationale: It says calculation work was automated and mathematicians could focus on other activities.

r002.rationale: It discusses automating calculations, but does not say that automating mathematical proofs could free mathematicians to formulate questions or theories.

r003.rationale: It explains that an activity that seemed central to mathematics was only one part of the work, and that a job contains multiple activities.
